terms.gloss: the hours of the working day
terms.grammar: hōra, hōrae f. with negōtiōsus, negōtiōsa, negōtiōsum
evidence: Tac. Ann. 13.41: dīvidī sacrōs et negōtiōsōs diēs
terms.comment: A description of ours, on the pattern of Tacitus’s negōtiōsī diēs, working days as against holy days. We have found no set phrase for working hours in Lewis & Short, Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini. Martial counts the Roman working day off by its hours instead (see the examples); for a working day see “weekday”.

phrases.latin: Prīma salūtantēs atque altera conterit hōra, exercet raucōs tertia causidicōs, in quīntam variōs extendit Rōma labōrēs, sexta quiēs lassīs, septima fīnis erit
phrases.english: The first hour and the second wear out the morning callers, the third keeps the hoarse advocates busy, Rome stretches her various labours into the fifth, the sixth is rest for the weary, the seventh will be the end.

phrases.latin: eōque oportēre dīvidī sacrōs et negōtiōsōs diēs, quīs dīvīna colerent et hūmāna nōn impedīrent
phrases.english: and that therefore holy days and working days should be kept apart, so that they might worship the gods without hindering human business

phrases.latin: Hōrīs negōtiōsīs in tablīnō sum; posteā lūdēmus.
phrases.english: During working hours I’m in the study; afterwards we’ll play.

sources: Lewis & Short: hora · Lewis & Short: negotiosus
